The following additional facts are known about the schedule of games in the tournament.
1. Each team played against a team from the other group in Round 8.
2. In Round 4 and Round 7, the match-ups, that is the pair of teams playing against each other, were identical. In Round 5 and Round 8, the match-ups were identical.
3. Team 4 played Team 6 in both Round 1 and Round 2.
4. Team 1 played Team 5 ONLY once and that was in Round 2.

6. In Round 8, Team 3 played Team 6, while Team 2 played Team 5.
questions.question_text: How many rounds were there in the tournament?

We are told that there are six teams, that are divided into two groups.
Teams in the same group will play each other only once, and teams in different group will play each other twice.
Calculating the combinations, there is going to be $^3C_2$ games among teams in the same group among them, and since there is two groups, total such games will be 6.
Now, teams in different group play each other twice. Calculating the combinations for this,
From the first group, a team can be chosen in three ways, and from the second group, a team can be chosen in three ways. Total ways two teams from different groups can play each other is 3x3 which is 9. And since they play each other twice, that is 9+9 games of this combination.
Total number of games is 18+6=24
It is given that each team plays one game in each round, that means there is going to be 3 matchups in each round. And given, there is 24 games to played in this format, the number of rounds will be 24/3=8
The tournament will have 8 rounds.

It is also known that Teams 2 and 3 are the only ones in stations E and D respectively at 10:00 hrs, and Team 1 and Team 4 are the only teams that patrol the street connecting stations A and E.

3. Hokli could not sell any item on the second day because the first household he met on that day complained against him.

In statement 1, it is given that all three of them met the same total number of households, and each of them sold a total of 100 items in two days. a + a + 30 = 2x
a + 15 = x
a = x - 15

$x=\frac{1500}{100-y}$

y = 40 and x = 25

Each of the bottles mentioned in this question contains 50 ml of liquid. The liquid in any bottle can be 100% pure content (P) or can have certain amount of impurity (I). Visually it is not possible to distinguish between P and I. There is a testing device which detects impurity, as long as the percentage of impurity in the content tested is 10% or more.
For example, suppose bottle 1 contains only P, and bottle 2 contains 80% P and 20% I. If content from bottle 1 is tested, it will be found out that it contains only P. If content of bottle 2 is tested, the test will reveal that it contains some amount of I. If 10 ml of content from bottle 1 is mixed with 20 ml content from bottle 2, the test will show that the mixture has impurity, and hence we can conclude that at least one of the two bottles has I. However, if 10 ml of content from bottle 1 is mixed with 5 ml of content from bottle 2. the test will not detect any impurity in the resultant mixture.
questions.question_text: 5 ml of content from bottle A is mixed with 5 ml of content from bottle B. The resultant mixture, when tested, detects the presence of I. If it is known that bottle A contains only P, what BEST can be concluded about the volume of I in bottle B?
questions.solution_text:
Given that each of the bottles contains a volume of 50 ml each.
If 5 ml from bottle A which contains only P is mixed with 5 ml of bottle B and in the resultant mixture the presence of I was detected.
In order to detect the presence of I in this, there must be at least 10% impurity in the 10 ml which is equivalent to 1 ml. This must be from bottle B.
Hence 5 ml of solution from B must contain at least 1ml of impurity and since bottle B is of a total volume of 50 ml. This must contain at least 10 ml of impurity.

questions.question_text: There are four bottles. Each bottle is known to contain only P or only I. They will be considered to be “collectively ready for despatch” if all of them contain only P. In minimum how many tests, is it possible to ascertain whether these four bottles are “collectively ready for despatch”?
questions.solution_text:
The bottles contain either P(pure) or I(impure). The possible cases here are :
1- (P, P, P, P), 2-(P,P,P,I), 3-(P,P,I,I), 4-(P,I,I,I), 5-(I,I,I,I).
In the first case if all the four solutions are pure then taking equal volumes of all the four bottles will get the result to dispatch or not to dispatch.

Among those appearing for CET, those at or above the 80th percentile in at least two sections, and at or above the 90th percentile overall, are selected for Advanced Entrance Test (AET) conducted by AIE. For the 200 candidates who are at or above the 90th percentile overall based on CET, the following are known about their performance in CET:

4. Number of candidates below 80th percentile in P: Number of candidates below 80th percentile in C: Number of candidates below 80th percentile in M = 4:2:1.BIE uses a different process for selection. If any candidate is appearing in the AET by AIE, BIE considers their AET score for final selection provided the candidate is at or above the 80th percentile in P. Any other candidate at or above the 80th percentile in P in CET, but who is not eligible for the AET, is required to appear in a separate test to be conducted by BIE for being considered for final selection. Altogether, there are 400 candidates this year who are at or above the 80th percentile in P.
questions.question_text: If the number of candidates who are at or above the 90th percentile overall and also are at or above the 80th percentile in P in CET, is more than 100, how many candidates had to sit for the separate test for BIE?

It is given that 200 candidates scored above 90th percentile overall in CET. Let the following Venn diagram represent the number of persons who scored above 80 percentile in CET in each of the three sections:

From (1), n = 0
From (2), d + e + f = 150
From (3), a = b = c
Since, there are a total of 200 candidates
a + b + c + g = 200 - 150 = 50
3a + g = 50 => a < 17
From (4), (b + f + c) : (a + d + b) : (a + e + c) = 4 : 2: 1
Or (2a + f) : (2a + d) : (2a + e) = 4 : 2 : 1
or, 6a + (d + e + f) = 7x
Or, 6a + 150 = 7x
So, a can be 3 or 10
x can be 24 or 30
2a + e can be 24 or 30 => e can be 18 or 10
2a + d can be 48 or 60 = > d can be 42 or 40
2a + f can be 96 or 120 => f can be 90 or 100
3a + g = 50 => g can be 41 or 20
Among the candidates who are at or above 90th percentile, the candidates who are at or above 80th percentile in at least two sections are selected for AET. Hence, the candidates represented by d, e, f and g are selected for AET.
BIE will consider the candidates who are appearing for AET and are at or above 80th percentile in P. Hence, BIE will consider the candidates represented by d, e and g, which can be 104 or 80.
BIE will conduct a separate test for the other students who are at or above 80th percentile in P. Given that there are a total of 400 candidates at or above 80th percentile in P, and since there are 104 or 80 candidates at or above 80th percentile in P and are at or above 90th percentile overall, there must be 296 or 320 candidates at or above 80th percentile in P who scored less than 90th percentile overall.
From the given condition, the number of candidates at or above 90th percentile overall and at or above 80th percentile in P in CET = (3 + 18 + 42 + 41) = 104.
The number of candidates who have to sit for separate test = (400 - 104 + 3) = 296 + 3 = 299 (we have added 3 for those who have scored more than 80th percentile only in P which is ‘a’).

The underlying principle that they are working on is the following:
Any person staying in any of these 10 cities should be able to make a trip to any other city in the morning and should be able to return by the evening of the same day.

Suppose the 10 cities are divided into 4 distinct groups G1, G2, G3, G4 having 3, 3, 2 and 2 cities respectively and that G1 consists of cities named A, B and C. Further, suppose that direct flights are allowed only between two cities satisfying one of the following:
1. Both cities are in G1
2. Between A and any city in G2 
3. Between B and any city in G3 
4. Between C and any city in G4
Then the minimum number of direct flights that satisfies the underlying principle of the airline is:
questions.solution_text:
In G1, we have three cities namely A, B, C. Person living in any of these three cities should be able to travel to other city once in the morning nad one in the night.  Therefore, a total of 4 flights are required between a pair of cities. 
A ---> B (Morning flight)
A ---> B (Evening flight)
B ---> A (Morning flight)
B ---> A (Evening flight)

Number of flights between the cities of G1 = 3c2*4 = 12
Between cities in A and any city in G2 = 3*4 = 12
Between B and any city in G3 = 2*4 = 8
Between C and any city in G4 = 2*4 = 8
Total = 12*2 + 8*2 = 40

All three daughters can't get 1-1 flat each as well. In that case, the daughter who owns 1 flat and the house will have assets worth 30+50 = 80 lakhs which is more than the actual share. Hence, we can conclude the one of the three daughter gets 2 flats and 10 lakhs bank deposit.

When an employee first joins the lab, her fingers are scanned in an order of her choice, and then when she wants to re-enter the facility, she has to scan the five fingers in the same sequence.
The lab authorities are considering some relaxations of the scan order requirements, since it is observed that some employees often get locked-out because they forget the sequence.
questions.question_text:
The lab has decided to allow a variation in the sequence of scans of the five fingers so that at most two scans (out of five) are out of place. For example, if the original sequence is Thumb (T), index finger (I), middle finger (M), ring finger (R) and little finger (L) then TLMRI is also allowed, but TMRLI is not.
How many different sequences of scans are allowed for any given person's original scan?
questions.solution_text:
Let the original sequence be TIMRL

Two fingers can be out of place. This can be done if and only if two fingers interchange their position. These two can be selected in $^5C_2 = 10$ ways. In addition to these, the original sequence will also be accepted. Hence the total number of acceptable sequences = 10 + 1 = 11

questions.passage_text: In a large forest, there are two large perpendicular highways, Highway A and Highway B, which are used by a firetruck to put off forest fires. The firetruck can travel at a speed of 50 Km/hr on the highways and it can travel at a speed of 10 Km/hr in the open forest. To reach a point in the forest, the firetruck can either travel along the highways or perpendicular to the highways.
questions.question_text: Suppose the firetruck is on Highway A (and very far away from Highway B). What is the area of the region that can be reached by the firetruck within an hour?
questions.solution_text:
Let us assume that the firetruck was initially at point O and the highway A is the X axis (line C-O-B). 

Within one hour, if the firetruck goes into the forest along line OA, it travels for a maximum of 10 Km.
If however, it continues travelling along the highway A, it covers a maximum of 50 Km.

questions.question_text: On a particular day, Ramlal starts his deliveries from city A and has to make deliveries to each city. What is the minimum distance he must travel to visit each city exactly once and return to city A without using the same road twice?
questions.solution_text:
Starting from city A, eight routes can be taken to visit each city exactly once and return to city A.
If the first city visited after A is B, then the following four routes are possible:
1. A-B-F-G-D-E-C-A --> total distance = 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 6 + 4 + 8 = 54km
2. A-B-F-G-E-D-C-A --> total distance = 6 + 7 + 11 + 8 + 6 + 3 + 8 = 49km
3. A-B-F-E-G-D-C-A --> total distance = 6 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 12 + 3 + 8 = 49km
4. A-B-E-F-G-D-C-A --> total distance = 6 + 9 + 5 + 11 + 12 + 3 + 8 = 54km
If the first city visited after A is C, then all the above routes in the reverse order are possible:
1. A-C-D-G-F-E-B-A --> total distance = 54km
2. A-C-D-G-E-F-B-A --> total distance = 49km
3. A-C-D-E-G-F-B-A --> total distance = 49km
4. A-C-E-D-G-F-B-A --> total distance = 54km
Thus, we can observe that the minimum distance that must be travelled to visit each city once is 49km.
Hence, option C is the correct answer.

A company evaluates its employees across six performance metrics: Quality of Work, Punctuality, Communication Skills, Problem-Solving Ability, Teamwork, and Leadership Skills. Each employee’s performance is rated on a scale of 1 to 10 for each metric. The  chart below shows the ratings of three employees (A, B, and C) across these metrics. 

Each metric is assigned a weight that reflects its importance in the overall performance evaluation. The weights for Quality of Work, Punctuality, Communication Skills are 0.6 and for the other three parameters, it is 0.4. The weighted score for any person is the weighted average of the individual ratings.

For example, if Quality of Work is rated 8, its contribution to the weighted score would be 8 × 0.6 = 4.8. The sum of the individual contributions would be the total weighted score. This total weighted score divided by the sum of weights would give the weighted average score.

A bonus (in Rs.) is given to each employee based on the weighted score i.e. Bonus = Weighted Average Score × 1000
questions.question_text: What is the highest weighted average rating among the three employees?
questions.solution_text:
We can make the following table mentioning the ratings received by all three employees in each parameters. 
Weighted average rating for A = $\dfrac{\left(\left(10+6+5\right)\times0.6+\left(9+8+7\right)\times0.4\right)}{3\times0.6+3\times0.4}=7.4$
Weighted average rating for B = $\dfrac{\left(\left(6+8+10\right)\times0.6+\left(7+6+8\right)\times0.4\right)}{3\times0.6+3\times0.4}=7.6$
Weighted average rating for C = $\dfrac{\left(\left(9+7+8\right)\times0.6+\left(6+8+10\right)\times0.4\right)}{3\times0.6+3\times0.4}=8$
With this, we can say, the highest rating received by anyone is 8.

A person named “ROBEN” is a believer in Numerology.

He number-coded each letter of the alphabet as: A-1, B-2, C-3, … Z-26.

His wife's name has some numeric properties:

1) It is a five lettered word with no letters repeated.

2) Only the alphabet ‘N’ is common between his and his wife’s names.

3) The product of the number codes of the letters of both their names is the same.

4) The name does not have the alphabet ‘A’

5) The fourth letter from the left is the second smallest and if it is removed from the word, all the remaining letters are in alphabetical order.
questions.question_text: What is the number code for the first letter of his wife’s name?
questions.solution_text:
The product of letters of the husband ROBEN is 18*15*2*5*14 = $2^3*3^3*5^2*7$.
The same should be the product of letters of the wife’s name. 
We know that the alphabet ‘N’ is common.
So we have the value 14 now.
We need to get $3^3$ from the wife’s name. 
27 as an alphabet is not possible. 
We should either have three multiples of 3 or one multiple of 9 and one multiple of 3. 
Let’s assume there are three multiples of 3.
They can be from 3, 6, 12, 15, 18, 21and 24.
But 15 and 18 are letters in the husband’s name and they can be eliminated.
21 has an extra 7 and can be eliminated. 
We already have the alphabet with code 14 and if we have the alphabet with code 24 there will be $2^4$ which should not be.
So we are left with only 3, 6 and 12.
If all three of 3, 6 and 12 are present then we will again have $2^4$ which should not be there.
So in the wife’s name there must be two letters one a multiple of 9 and another a multiple of 3.
As 18 is already there in the husband’s name the wife’s name must have 9.
Now 14 and 9 are there and we must find the other 3 letters whose product must be $2^2*3*5^2$
There must be two 5s in her name. They can be in the form of two multiples of 5 or as 25.
If they are as two multiples of 5 they can be from among 5, 10, 15 and 20.
But 5 and 15 are already present in the husband’s name.
So only 10 and 20 are possible.
If 10 and 20 both cannot be present as then we will have $2^4$ in the wife’s name which should not be.
So 25 must be present in the wife’s name.
Now we have three letters 14, 9 and 25. The product of the remaining two numbers is 12.
They can be of the form (1, 12), (2, 6) and (3, 4).
(1, 12) cannot be because it is given that the letter A is not a part of her name. 
(2, 6) cannot be because the alphabet B is already present in the husband’s name.
So the only possibility is (3, 4).
So the letters in her name are 14, 9, 25, 3 and 4 which are N, I, Y, C and D.
It is given that if the fourth letter from the left is shifted to second from the left then all the letters are in alphabetical order.
So her name must be “CINDY”.

For eg) If Agarwal makes a Gulab Jamun on Monday, it expires by Tuesday night. Agarwal cannot sell a sweet that has expired. Therefore, every night, he throws away the sweets that have expired and keeps only the sweets that have not expired in stock. questions.question_text: What is the profit earned by Agarwal in the entire week?
questions.solution_text:
We know that Agarwal did not have any sweet in stock by the beginning of Monday and by the end of Friday. Also, we know that Gulab Jamun and Cham Cham expire in 2 days and Jalebi expires in 3 days. 

50 Gulab Jamuns were made on Monday. 30 Gulab Jamuns were sold on Monday. 20 Gulab Jamuns will be in stock. Now, on Tuesday, 30 Gulab Jamuns were sold. 20 Gulab Jamuns from Monday and 10 Gulab Jamuns from Tuesday will be sold on Tuesday. The remaining 30 Gulab Jamuns from Tuesday will be stocked. 

Now, on Wednesday 10 Gulab Jamuns are sold and 30 Gulab Jamuns are made. The Gulab Jamuns made on Tuesday, if not sold on Wednesday, will expire. Therefore, Agarwal will sell 10 Gulab Jamuns from Tuesday’s stock. The remaining 20 Gulab Jamuns from Tuesday’s stock will expire. Now, Agarwal has only 30 Gulab Jamuns left from Wednesday’s stock. 

On Thursday, 20 Gulab Jamuns were made and 30 were sold. All 30 Gulab Jamuns sold will be from Wednesday’s stock. 20 Gulab Jamuns from Thursday’s stock will remain by the end of Thursday.

On Friday, 20 Gulab Jamuns were made and 40 were sold. All 20 Gulab Jamuns from Thursday’s stock and all 20 Gulab Jamuns made on Friday will be sold. 

Constructing a table using the inferences, we get,

We can construct similar tables for Cham Cham and Jalebi (Jalebi expires on the third day)

Total revenue of Agarwal:

Total revenue = (30+30+10+30+40)*20 + (20+30+15+15+30)*22 + (25+10+10+15+40)*20 = 2800+2420 +2000

Total revenue = Rs.7220.

Total cost that Agarwal spent on Storage:

We know that it costs Rs. 1 to store a Jalebi and Rs.2 to store a Gulab Jamun and Cham Cham. 

Amount spent on Monday = 2*20 + 2*20 + 25 = Rs.105 
 Amount spent on Tuesday = 2*30 + 2*10 + 45 = Rs.125
Amount spent on Wednesday = 2*30 + 2*25 + 50 = Rs.160

Amount spent on Thursday = 2*20 + 2*10 + 30 = Rs.90

Total amount spent on Storage = Rs.105+125+160+90 = Rs.480.

Total cost incurred in making the sweets:

Total cost that Agarwal incurred in making the sweets = (50+40+30+20+20)*10 + (40+20+30+10+20)*15 + (50+30+20+10+10)*12
                                                                                  = 160*10 + 120*15 + 120*12
                                                                                  = 1600 + 1800 + 1440
                                                                                  = Rs.4840

=> Profit earned by Agarwal in the week = Revenue - Cost of making the sweet - Storage cost
                                                            = 7220 - 4840-480
Profit earned by Agarwal                    = Rs.1900

Jayaraj owns an empty plot and 62 gold coins. The empty plot is worth 100 gold coins. As he is turning old, Jayaraj wants to distribute his assets to his sons. He has 5 sons Arun, Bikram, Charan, Dinesh, and Edward. He likes his eldest son Arun more than the other four and hence, wants to give Arun the plot he owns. However, the other 4 sons expressed their disapproval over the decision. Jayaraj decided to devise a game and rig it in favour of Arun. He made his sons stand in the form of a circle and distributed the 62 gold coins to them such that the number of coins with the sons form a geometric progression.

Jayaraj laid down the rules of the game as follows:

In each round, every person should give exactly half the number of coins with him to the person standing to his immediate right. If the number of coins with a person at the end of a round is odd, the person gets eliminated and steps out of the circle. The person who is eliminated takes the gold coins he has with him. The game progresses in multiple rounds and the person who does not get eliminated till the end gets the plot. Jayaraj distributed the coins in such a way that Arun gets the plot.

Further, the following observations were made after the first round ended.

The number of coins with 4 of the 5 persons are in a geometric progression after the end of first round (before anyone steps out of circle). Charan and Edward are the persons who got eliminated after the first round. Charan took more coins with him than Edward. At the end of the game, Dinesh had less number of coins than Bikram. Dinesh and Bikram are not sitting beside each other at the start.
questions.question_text: Who was standing 2 places to the right of Edward in the first round?
questions.solution_text:
64 coins are distributed in such a way that the number of coins with each son forms a geometric progression. 

Let the coins with the sons be $a, ar, ar^2, ar^3,$ and $ar^4$.
$a+ar+ar^2+ar^3+ar^4 = 62$
$a*(1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4) = 62$
We know that both $a$ and $r$ are integers. 
(1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4) should be an odd number.
62 = 2*31
=> a =2 and $1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4 = 31$
$a=2$ and $r=2$

The number of coins with the 5 persons are 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32. 
We know that each person has to give half the number of coins with him to the person standing to the immediate right. It has also been given that if the number of coins with a person cannot be divided into 2 halves ( i.e, the number of coins with a person is odd), the person gets eliminated from the tournament. 

The person with 2 coins will definitely get eliminated in the first round. The person with 2 coins will keep one coin with him and hand over the other coin to the person standing to his immediate right. All the other numbers (4, 8, 16, and 32), on division by 2, yield an even number. Therefore, the person who had 2 coins will receive an even number of coins. Since even+odd= odd, the person with 2 coins will be eliminated by the end of the first round. The person who receives one coin from the person who has 2 coins will also get eliminated (Since the person will have either 2, 4, 8 or 16 coins after giving half of his coins and receiving 1 coin will make the total number of coins odd). 

=> Charan and Edward are the person who had 2 coins and the person who stood to the immediate right of the person who had 2 coins in any order.

The number of coins with 4 of the five persons were in a geometric progression. 

Each person will receive one among 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 coins. Each person will give one among 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 coins. 

All of them cannot give and receive the same number of coins. 
Now, the number of coins with the persons is already in a geometric progression.
Therefore, the net gain or loss of coins for the 4 persons should also be a geometric progression with the same common factor. 

Since the number of coins given and the number of coins received are already in a geometric progression (with same common ratio), offsetting the first terms will yield us another geometric progression with the same common ratio.

Therefore, the net gain/loss of coins for the 4 persons whose coins (number of coins) are in a geometric progression should be 2-1 = 1, 4-2 = 2, 8-4 = 4, 16-8 = 8, and 1-16 = -15. 

The person whose net gain/loss is odd will be the persons who will be eliminated after the first round. 

We know that Charan and Edward are the persons who got eliminated. Since we know that neither Charan nor Edward had 32 coins initially, we know that the -15 denotes a net gain of 15 coins and the 1 denotes a net loss of 1 coin (Since only the person with 32 coins could have given 16 coins).

The number of coins with the 5 persons initially - 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
Net loss of coins in the given order  - -15, 1, 2, 4, 8.
Number of coins by the end of round 1 - 17, 3, 6, 12, 24.
Number of coins with Charan by the end of round 1 - 17
Number of coins with Edward by the end of round 1 - 3

Arun, Bikram, and Dinesh will progress to the second round. 
Now, we know that Arun won the game. 
The number of coins with the 3 persons are 6, 12, 24. 
The person with 6 coins and the person standing to the immediate right of the person with 6 coins will get eliminated (since the person with 6 coins will give 3 coins, eliminating himself and the person standing to his right).

Since Arun won the plot, he cannot be the person having 6 coins or the person standing to the immediate right of the person with 6 coins. Arun should be standing to the immediate right of the person with 12 coins. 

Arun should have had 24 coins with him. He would have given 12 coins and received 6 coins. By the end of round 2, Arun would have won the plot and walked away with 24-12+6 = 18 gold coins. 

The person with 6 gold coins would have given 3 coins and received 12 coins. Therefore, the person with 6 gold coins would have ended up with 15 coins. 

The person with 12 gold coins would have given 6 coins and received 3 coins. Therefore, the person with 12 gold coins would have ended up with 9 coins. Since Dinesh took away fewer coins than Bikram, Dinesh should have ended up with 9 coins and Bikram should have ended up with 15 coins. 

The final results are as follows:

Arun - Plot + 18 gold coins (Winner of the second round)
Bikram - 15 gold coins (Eliminated in the second round)
Charan - 17 gold coins (Eliminated in the first round)
Dinesh - 9 gold coins (Eliminated in the second round)
Edward - 3 gold coins (Eliminated in the first round)

Bikram was standing 2 places to the right of Edward in the first round and hence, option A is the right answer.

64 coins are distributed in such a way that the number of coins with each son forms a geometric progression.

$a+ar+ar^2+ar^3+ar^4 = 62$
$a*(1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4) = 62$
We know that both $a$ and $r$ are integers. 
($1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4$) should be an odd number.
62 = 2*31
=> a =2 and $1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4 = 31$
$a=2$ and $r=2$

The number of coins with the 5 persons are 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32. 
We know that each person has to give half the number of coins with him to the person standing to the immediate right. It has also been given that if the number of coins with a person cannot be divided into 2 halves ( i.e, the number of coins with a person is odd), the person gets eliminated from the tournament. 

The person with 2 coins will definitely get eliminated in the first round. The person with 2 coins will keep one coin with him and hand over the other coin to the person standing to his immediate right. All the other numbers (4, 8, 16, and 32), on division by 2, yield an even number. Therefore, the person who had 2 coins will receive an even number of coins. Since even+odd= odd, the person with 2 coins will be eliminated by the end of the first round. The person who receives one coin from the person who has 2 coins will also get eliminated (Since the person will have either 2, 4, 8 or 16 coins after giving half of his coins and receiving 1 coin will make the total number of coins odd).

Each person will receive one among 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 coins. Each person will give one among 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 coins. 

All of them cannot give and receive the same number of coins. 
Now, the number of coins with the persons is already in a geometric progression.
Therefore, the net gain or loss of coins for the 4 persons should also be a geometric progression with the same common factor. 

Since the number of coins given and the number of coins received are already in a geometric progression (with same common ratio), offsetting the first terms will yield us another geometric progression with the same common ratio.

Therefore, the net gain/loss of coins for the 4 persons whose coins (number of coins) are in a geometric progression should be 2-1 = 1, 4-2 = 2, 8-4 = 4, 16-8 = 8, and 1-16 = -15. 

The person whose net gain/loss is odd will be the persons who will be eliminated after the first round. 

We know that Charan and Edward are the persons who got eliminated. Since we know that neither Charan nor Edward had 32 coins initially, we know that the -15 denotes a net gain of 15 coins and the 1 denotes a net loss of 1 coin (Since only the person with 32 coins could have given 16 coins).

questions.passage_text:
While roaming an exo-planet, we have encountered a set of mysterious particles with a charge associated with them. The charge can be any integer.

We observe that there are ‘n’ such particles in a straight line, and they display the following properties.

1) When we touch a particle that is not at the ends, it disappears, and the two particles adjacent to them combine to form a single particle with a charge equal to the sum of the charges of adjacent elements.

2) When we touch a particle on the ends, it disappears.

For example, Let us say we have 5 such particles with charges (-3,1,-4,7,2).
When we touch the 2nd particle from the left, the set becomes -7,7,2. (-3 and -4 combine to form -7).
When we touch the particle at the right end, the set becomes -7,7. (2 disappears).

Noting these properties, we have to perform the above operations such that after all our operations, one mysterious particle remains (Omega-Particle), and its charge is as high as possible (numerically, not just the magnitude), i.e. we perform operations in such a way that it maximises the charge of the final particle remaining.
questions.question_text: Suppose the set of mysterious particles we encounter is {5, 2, 7, 4, 3, 1}. Find the charge of the Omega-Particle.
questions.solution_text:
1st Observation:
By doing any set of operations in any order, we can never combine two particles that are adjacent to each other.
That is, we can only combine the particles whose place parity is the same. Simply put, we can only combine the elements in odd or even places.
Example:
Let’s consider the set, {1,4,-5,7,10}
By removing the 2nd particle, we combine the 1st and 3rd particles. Can we combine 1st and 5th particles by performing some operations?
Yes, First select the 3rd element => The set becomes 1,4+7,10
Now, select the 3rd element in the above set => set becomes 1+10 = 11.
Using this observation that it is possible to combine selected particles at even or odd places, let's extrapolate the idea to when negative particles are present. 
Can we skip the negative elements contributing to the final charge of the omega particle? Yes.
Let’s consider the {1,-3,-4,5,7}
From the above observation, we see that we can combine particles of odd or even indices, i.e. 1,-4,7 can be combined, or -3,5 can be combined.
There is a way where we can avoid (-4) contributing to the final omega particle.
First select the 3nd particle => 1, -3+5, 7 => 1,2,7
Now select the 2nd particle => 1+7 => 8.
So, In a general set where the particles are as follows {a,b,-c,-d,e,f,g}
We can either arrive at the sum of positive elements at odd places or the sum of positive particles at even places. i.e. we calculate (a + e + g) and (b+f) and see which is greater, and we can arrive at that value.
Let’s say b + f is greater.
remove -d => a,b,e-c,f,g
remove e-c => a,b+f,g
remove a => b+f,g
remove g => b+f.
Let’s say a+e+g is greater.
remove -c => a,b-d,e,f,g
remove b-d => a+e,f,g
remove f => a+e+g.
Effectively, we can obtain the sum of all positive particles in either even or odd places, and the maximum of both will be the charge of the omega particle.
There is one corner case to consider here.
What if all the elements are negative:
Let’s say the set is {-a,-b,-c,-d,-e,-f}. Combining any two particles will only reduce the sum of the charge of the omega particle; we just remove particles such that the particle with the highest charge among the particles is present.
From the above explanation, we can arrive at max(5+7+3,2+4+1) = 15.

remove -d => a,b,e-c,f,g

remove a => b+f,g

Raghav have a cube with volume 729 $cm^3$, and which is painted with red colour on the outer surface area. He cuts the cube into 27 small cubes and coloured all the unpainted faces blue. 
Further the all the smaller cubes are cut to make cubes of 1 cm$^3$ and all the unpainted walls are painted black.
questions.question_text: How many cubes have all the walls painted black?
questions.solution_text:
The following diagram represents the process given in the question:
The large cube is of a dimension 9*9*9. This is cut into 27 medium cubes of dimension 3*3*3 and each of these medium cubes is cut into 27 cubes of dimension of 1*1*1. Hence 1 large cube => 27 medium cubes => 729 small cubes.
Of these small 729 cubes, we have to find those that are painted entirely black. The cube will be painted entirely black if it was not on the surface in either the large cube or the medium cube. Any cube that was on the surface in large cube would by default be on the surface in medium cube. So we have to find how many cubes are internal cubes in each medium cube. 
Number of internal cubes in a cube of side n = $(n-2)^3$ = $(3-2)^3$ = 1
Hence, each of the 27 medium cubes will have one cube which will not be painted red or blue. Thus, it will be entirely black. Thus, we have 27 entirely black cubes.

Four friends - P, Q, R and S - play a guessing game. S is the taskmaster and presents his friends with a list of 20 dates. He picks one specific date and writes down the correct month on paper P1, the correct year on paper P2 and the correct day on paper P3. S folds these paper pieces and distributes them as follows: P gets P1, Q gets P3, and R gets P2. While all three of them know the kind of paper the others possess, none of them is allowed to openly disclose the information written on the paper. If all of them guess the date correctly, then S is eliminated. The following conversation ensues among the three friends:

P states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that Q doesn’t know it.
Q states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that R doesn’t know it.
R states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that P still doesn’t know it.
P exclaims: I know the date now!
Q exclaims: So do I!

Since everyone guessed the date correctly, S is out of the game and R is made the new taskmaster. Surprisingly, she states that one of the dates on the list is her birthday. To help P and Q figure out this date, R states that the correct month is one out of June, July, October and November. Further, she secretly tells P the correct month and Q the correct day. Both P and Q are told that they each have one correct piece of information about the birthdate. The following conversation ensues:

R states: Q doesn’t know the correct date. 
P states: I don’t know the correct date either. 
Q exclaims: I know R’s birthdate now!
P exclaims: So do I!

List of Dates:
questions.question_text: The months are arranged from May to December in the order of their occurrence and numbered from 1 to 8. Enter the number that corresponds to the correct month of the specific date given by S.
questions.solution_text:
Rearranging the dates by month, we can create the following table:
P - correct month; Q - correct day ; R - correct year
P states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that Q doesn’t know it.
The only way P can be confident about Q not knowing the correct date is if the day is not a unique value. We notice that August 11, 1995, and October 12, 1994, are the only unique values in the table and had S told Q either of these two numbers, Q would have been able to quickly guess the correct date. P can be sure that these two dates are incorrect since the month S told him was different, i.e. he was informed of a month other than August and October. Hence, we can remove all the dates belonging to these months. We get the following modified table: 
Q states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that R doesn’t know it.
Since Q can still not determine the correct date, any other unique day value can be eliminated. We notice that June 17, 1993, and September 15, 1993, are unique values in the modified table and had S told Q either of these two numbers, Q would have been able to correctly guess the date by now. However, this is not the case. Therefore, these two dates can be removed.
We also notice that July 23, 1993, is the only date from the year 1993 and had this been the correct year value, R would have been able to guess the date by now. Since this is not the case, we can deduce that 1993 is not the correct year. With this, we also understand that 23 cannot be the correct day, and thus, May 23, 1995, can also be removed. Hence, we get the following table:
R states: I don’t know the correct date, but I know that P still doesn’t know it.
Since R claims that P is still unable to figure out the correct date, we identify that P cannot have a month that appears only once in the table - this would be May. If the correct date was May 19, 1996, P would have guessed it by now. Hence, we can remove this date. With this, we also deduce that 1996 is not the correct year; therefore, all dates in this year can be eliminated as a possible answer [R is confident that P doesn’t know the correct date because he knows that 1996 is not the correct year]. We obtain the following table: 
P exclaims: I know the date now!
Q exclaims: So do I!
Since P now knows the correct date, it has to be from one of the months with a single date remaining {i.e. from June, September, November or December}. However, we notice that only one out of the four dates is unique: September 24, 1994. If it were any other date, Q would not be able to figure it out.

Each of the six friends is married to exactly one out of six females namely-Pinky, Queen, Rashi, Sonal, Tanu, and Urmi. On 30th Sept 2018, it was a Sunday and Ramesh recalled the following points: 

1. He attended the marriages on four different dates among 19th Jan, 12th March, 18th April and 25th June. There are exactly two pairs of friends whose marriage was on the same date but in different years.

2. Both Bimal and Eshaan were married on the same day of week but in different years. Eshaan has been married for a longer period of time than Bimal. 

3. Both Pinky and Queen were married on the same day of week in the same year. Pinky has been married for a longer period of time than Queen.

questions.passage_text: ABC Coaching classes conducted a test of the class X students of a school for admission in their coaching institute. The test consisted of 32 questions in each subject. A student scored 4 marks on answering a question correctly and lost 1 mark for answering a question incorrectly. Leaving a question has no effect on the marks of the student. The marks of a student Prakash are given below. It is known that Prakash scored 62.50% of the maximum marks and attempted a total of 81.25% questions.
questions.question_text: In how many subjects did Prakash leave the more than 5 questions unattempted ?
questions.solution_text:
We need to try to tabulate the data given here
Maximum marks in the test = $4 \times 32 \times 5 = 640$ marks 
Marks scored by Prakash = $\dfrac{62.5}{100} \times 640 = 400$ marks 
(1) Thus, marks scored by Prakash in Maths = $\dfrac{23.75}{100} \times 400 = 95$ marks 
 Questions attempted correctly by Prakash in Maths=25
95=Number of correct questions*4-Number of incorrect questions*1
=> 95=25*4-Number of incorrect questions*1   => Number of incorrect questions in Maths = 5
Number of Unattempted questions in Maths= 32-25-5=2 
(2) Marks scored by Prakash in English = $\dfrac{23.75}{100} \times 400 = 95$ marks 
Questions attempted correctly by Prakash in English=24
95=Number of correct questions*4-Number of incorrect questions*1
=> 95=24*4-Number of incorrect questions*1   => Number of incorrect questions in English = 1
Number of Unattempted questions in English= 32-24-1=7
(3)Marks scored by Prakash in Physics = $\dfrac{20}{100} \times 400 = 80$ marks 
Questions attempted correctly by Prakash in Physics=22
80=Number of correct questions*4-Number of incorrect questions*1
=> 80=22*4-Number of incorrect questions*1   => Number of incorrect questions in Physics = 8
Number of Unattempted questions in Physics= 32-22-8=2
(4) Marks scored by Prakash in Chemistry = $\dfrac{12.50}{100} \times 400 = 50$ marks 
Questions attempted correctly by Prakash in Chemistry=14
50=Number of correct questions*4-Number of incorrect questions*1
=> 50=14*4-Number of incorrect questions*1   => Number of incorrect questions in Chemistry = 6
Number of Unattempted questions in Chemistry= 32-14-6=12
(5) Marks scored by Prakash in Physical Education = $\dfrac{20}{100} \times 400 = 80$ marks 
Questions attempted correctly by Prakash in Physical Education=21

The X- axis represents the time period. The area of a particular vegetable, between a chosen time period gives the quantity of the particular vegetable produced in that time period. 

In X axis, the line segment from 2015 to 2016 measures 100 units. In Y axis, the line segment from 0 to 20 measures 20 units.

1 sq unit area for a particular vegetable denotes 1kg production of that particular vegetable.

The values from the graph on the y axis are in multiples of 5.
questions.question_text: How many kgs of potatoes are produced in the time period between 2015 and 2017?
questions.solution_text:
We find that the area of the figure between any two given years would always be a trapezium. For example consider the time period between 2015 and 2016.
The lines x= 2015 and x= 2016 are parallel. Hence, opposite sides are parallel and the figure is a quadrilateral for any vegetable in between any two years.
Hence, the area would be found by the formula (height * average of parallel sides).

2015-2016 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(40+45\right)\cdot100\ =\ 4250$
2016-2017 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(45+50\right)\cdot100\ =\ 4750$
2017-2018 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(50+55\right)\cdot100\ =\ 5250$
2018-2019 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(55+95\right)\cdot100\ =\ 7500$
Tomato :

2016-2017 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(25+25\right)\cdot100\ =\ 2500$
2017-2018 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(25+35\right)\cdot100\ =\ 3000$
2018-2019 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(35+15\right)\cdot100\ =2500$
Beetroot:
2015-2016 :$\frac{1}{2}\left(50+60\right)\cdot100\ =5500$
2016-2017 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(60+75\right)\cdot100\ =\ 6750$
2017-2018 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(75+90\right)\cdot100\ =8250$
2018-2019 :$\frac{1}{2}\left(90+105\right)\cdot100\ =9750$
Cabbage:
2015-2016 :$\frac{1}{2}\left(20+35\right)\cdot100\ =2750$
2016-2017 : $\frac{1}{2}\left(35+25\right)\cdot100\ =\ 3000$
2017-2018 :$\frac{1}{2}\left(25+40\right)\cdot100\ =3250$
2018-2019 :$\frac{1}{2}\left(40+60\right)\cdot100\ =5000$

 Firm XYZ plans to hire potters through the association, and each potter requires a pottery wheel. The firm owns a certain number of wheels and will have to rent one for every additional potter they hire. The rent for each wheel is the same regardless of the number of wheels rented.

On hiring 20 potters, the company pays 6 rupees in rent, hence renting 3 wheels. 
Therefore, the company must have 17 wheels of their own. 
Therefore, 17 is the correct answer.

District Chenzen has three towns: A, B, and C. The following charts represent the percentage increase in the population, revenue, and number of shops in Chenzen over a 5-year span, with the second chart showing the contribution of towns A and B to the growth of the district over the given span of time. 

It is also known that for each year, each shop generates equal revenue, and every town member has an equal share in the number of shops in that town.
questions.question_text: What is the approximate percentage change in the average revenue generated by each shop from year 1 to year 5?
questions.solution_text:
Suppose the original number of shops was S and the original total revenue was R. 
This would give us the average revenue generated by the shops in year 1 as R/S
Over the span of five years the revenue changes to $\left(1.2\right)^2\left(1.3\right)\left(1.4\right)R$ while the number of shops change to $\left(1.1\right)^2\left(1.3\right)$S. 
Giving the average revenue to be $\frac{\left(1.2\right)^2\times\ 1.3\times\ 1.4}{1.1^2\times\ 1.3}\times\ \frac{R}{S}$
$\frac{1.44\times\ 1.4}{1.21}\times\ \frac{R}{S}=1.666\ \frac{R}{S}$
Hence the percentage change would be $\frac{\left(0.666\ \frac{R}{S}\right)}{\frac{R}{S}}\times\ 100=66.6\%$
The closest option is option B, 66%
Therefore, Option B is the correct answer.

ABC institute scheduled two seminars, one each on "Inflation 
Targeting" and "Women Empowerment in Informal Sector". The auditorium 
they had chosen for the seminar has sitting available for only 899 
people with that many chairs only arranged in the form of grid having 
dimensions $31\times29$. So the first 899 registered students are only allowed to attend the seminars. Each student was given a different registration number  from 1 to 899 at the time of registration. Also, it was mandatory for everyone to attend both the seminars and the same registration number is valid for both.

• Rows are numbered as row 1, row 2, row 3, ...... and row 31, and columns are numbered as column 1, column 2, column 3, ....., column 29.

• For "Inflation Targeting", students were asked to sit according to their registration number in row-wise manner. For example, student with registration number 1 sits on the seat in row 1 and column 1; student with registration number 2 sits on the seat in row 1 and column 2; and so on till registration number 29. Then student with registration number 30 sits on the seat in row 2 and column 1; student with registration number 31 sits on the seat in row 2 and column 2; and so on. And hence followed the same pattern till all the students got their seats.

• For "Women Empowerment in Informal Sector", students were asked to sit according to their registration number in column-wise manner. For example, student with registration number 1 sits on the seat in column 1 and row 1; student with registration number 2 sits on the seat in column 1 and row 2; and so on till registration number 31. Then student with registration number 32 sits on the seat in column 2 and row 1; the student with registration number 33 sits on the seat in column 2 and row 2; and so on. And hence followed the same pattern till all the students got their seats.
questions.question_text: How many students go on to seat on the same seat in both the seminars?
questions.solution_text:
Sitting arrangement of students during the seminar titled as “Inflation Targeting" is as given below, where number mentioned in any cell is the registration number of the student sitting on that seat.
If we observe the above table, we can see every row has consecutive numbers starting from 29×(row - 1) + 1.
So, the general term for the above table can be written as  $C_{ij}=29(i-1)+j,$ where $C_{ij}$ represents the seat in i th row and j th column.
Similarly, sitting arrangement of students during the seminar titled as “Women Empowerment in Informal Sector” is as given below
So, the general term for the above table can be written as $C_{ij}=31(j-1)+i$.
The student having same $C_{ij}$ value for both the seminars, got to sit on the same seat,
Therefore, $29\left(i-1\right)+j=31\left(j-1\right)+i$
or, $15j-14i=1$
Only possible positive integer solutions of the above equations are (1,1), (16,15) and (31,29).
Therefore, 3 students got to sit on same seat in both the seminars.

questions.solution_text:
To calculate the maximum number of students who failed in all the subjects of Exam 1, take a look at the subject which is having the highest average marks in exam 1 which is maths with the score of 94.
Total marks in maths = 20*94 = 1880
Suppose 2 students score 39 each.
Remaining marks = 1880-78 = 1802 which is not possible as maximum sum possible is 1800.
Hence at most only one student failed in maths and in all other subjects.

The following diagram shows the depth of 25 pits adjacent to each other (in cm).

There are 5 varieties of frogs - A, B, C, D, and E and the frogs of these varieties can leap 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm, 25 cm, and 35 cm vertically upwards respectively. Each frog can jump horizontally for more than the width of the entire set up. The vertical height to which the frog can jump prevents its movement from one pit to another. Also, a frog can jump and land on an adjacent pit if the difference between the height of the 2 pits is not more than the height that the frog can vertically jump. All frogs are rational and try to get to a shallower adjacent pit or try to get directly out of the set up. There are 5 frogs of each variety and the frogs are kept in these 25 pits such that no frog can get out of the pit in which it is kept. 2 pits are considered adjacent to each other if they share at least a side. 

No 2 frogs of variety B are kept in adjacent pits. The same is the case with frogs of variety C as well. All the frogs of type E have at least one frog of type A in an adjacent pit. No frog of variety B is kept in a pit adjacent to a pit in which a frog of variety E is kept. Also, no frog of variety D has frogs of variety B in all the adjacent pits. No frog of type D is kept in a pit such that it has to jump more than twice the height it can jump to get out of the pit.
questions.question_text: How many frogs of variety D have at least one frog of variety C in their adjacent pits?
questions.solution_text:
Since the frogs can get out of their pit even if the difference between the depths of one of the adjacent pits and the pit in which the frog is kept is less than the vertical height the frog can jump, the least difference between the heights of the pit in which the frog is kept and one of the adjacent pits will be the limiting factor. A metal alloy is made up of 4 metals Iron, Aluminum, Manganese and Cobalt. It comes in five different grades with each grade containing a different composition of these four metals. The composition (in percentage) has been shown in the form of a bar graph. The price per kg of each metal constituent has been shown from year 2012 and 2013 in the table. These alloys are used as raw materials in the aviation, automobile and shipbuilding industry.

It is known that:

1. Aviation industry always uses an alloy of higher aluminium composition than the shipbuilding industry. The automobile industry always uses an alloy with lower aluminium composition as compared to the shipbuilding industry.
2. During any given year, the price per kg of alloy used by the three industries decreases in the following order
      Shipbuilding industry>Aviation industry>Automobile industry
3. Each industry uses only one grade of an alloy during a given year.
questions.question_text: What is the maximum amount of aluminium that could be present in a 100kg block of alloy used by shipbuilding industry in 2013?
questions.solution_text:
Price of Grade 1 in 2012 will be (Sum(Price*percentage))/100 = (40*25+28*15+35*20+24*25)/100 = 2720/100 =27.2
Similarly , we can tabulate the price of the different grade of metals, we get
For price,  Shipbuilding industry> Aviation sector  > automobile industry
Aluminium Content, Aviation sector > shipbuilding industry > automobile industry
For year 2012, Shipbuilding industry, Aviation sector, automobile industry = (28.6,28.2,27.2)
For year 2013, Shipbuilding industry, Aviation sector, automobile industry = (20.75,20.5,19.9), (21,20.05,19.9)
The only possible combination is 
Shipbuilding : Grade 3/ Grade 4     Aviation : Grade 5     Automobile : Grade 2
In Grade 4, Aluminium is 35% composition.
If Shipbuilding industry uses grade 3, Aluminium will be 40%=  40kg in 100kg
Hence 40 kg is the answer.

questions.passage_text: Sohan appeared in the Catalyst Test for three years, 2017, 2018 and 2019. The test consists of six subjects, represented by S1, S2, S3, S4, S5 and S6. The following diagram represents the top three subjects and the marks obtained in those subjects in a particular year. The small circle in the middle represents the percentage of marks obtained in the top three subjects with respect to the total marks obtained in all the six subjects together in a year. Marks obtained in no two different subjects were equal in a particular year. (Assume that the marks obtained in each subject every year is always a positive integer)
questions.question_text: What is the maximum possible percentage increase in the marks in S3 from 2017 to 2019?
questions.solution_text:
The percentage given in the small circle represents the percentage of the total marks of the top three subjects with respect to the total marks in all the six subjects combined. Using this, we can calculate the total marks. Since the marks obtained in the top three subjects are given, the marks obtained in the other three subjects must be less than the minimum value of the marks obtained in the top three subjects. For example, in 2017, 50 marks were obtained in S6 and S6 was one of the top three subjects. So, the marks obtained in the remaining subjects must be less than 50. Thus, we can find the range in which the marks obtained in those subjects, which have not been provided, can lie. In the similar manner, we can calculate for 2018 and 2019 also. After calculating, we will get the following table:
Sohan got 85 marks in S3 in 2017. 
In 2019, we have to maximize the marks obtained in S3. For this, the marks obtained in S2 and S4 must be minimum. The marks obtained is always a positive integer. Also, no two different subjects have the same marks. So, the minimum marks obtained in S2 and S4 can be 1 and 2 in any order. However, if the marks obtained in S2 and S4 will be 1 and 2, the marks obtained in S3 will be (125 - 3) = 122 which is not possible as the maximum marks in S3 can be 104 only.
Therefore, the maximum marks obtained in S3 in 2019 can be 104.
The maximum possible percentage change = $\dfrac{104 - 85}{85} * 100$ = 22.35%
Hence, option B is the correct answer.

There is a box having nine cards with the numbers 1 to 9 written on them. Ravi picks up one card at a time, without being aware of the number and then places the numbers side by side to get a nine-digit code. Now, in the 9-digit code, if there is any number divisible by 2 immediately followed by a number divisible by 3, then this pair is called a rewarding pair. No two rewarding pairs can have a common number between them. Hence, if there are n rewarding pairs, there are 2n numbers among these pairs. At the end of the activity, Ravi is paid Rs 200 for each rewarding pair that the code has. If the code has 2 rewarding pairs, he is paid Rs 400, and so on. 

For example- The code 123456789 has two rewarding pairs -23- and -89-.

Based on the information, answer the questions that follow.
questions.question_text: If the final code is in the form of  __  2  __  __  __  6  __  __  9, how many codes are possible if Ravi wins Rs 600?
questions.solution_text:
Ravi gets three rewarding pairs. 
__  2  __  __  __  6  __  __  9
Now, only 'three' multiples of 3 are available, so we can have at most three rewarding pairs. Hence, all the multiples of 3 must come after a multiple of 2. Now, the number of multiples of 2 that are left is 3. Hence, the multiples of 2 come before a multiple of 3. 2 must be followed by 3. And 4 and 8 come before 6 and 9(in no particular order). Hence we get 2 cases.
__  2  3  __  4/8  6 __  4/8  9
Now, the remaining 3 spaces can be filled in 3! ways.
Hence a total of 2.3!, that is, twelve ways.

In a game of card cricket, there are cards placed on a table, each card having an identifiable front(F) and a back(B) side. The first card has number 1 on F and 2 on B, the second card has number 3 on F and 4 on B, and so on..... The nth card has 2n-1 on F and 2n on B. These cards are shuffled, such that the F of each card is on the top and the B of each card is on the bottom. The batsman picks up any random card in each turn. If the number on either F or B of the card has a single digit, the batsman is termed OUT. Else if the number on either F or B has every digit as the same(ex: 555, 66, 1111), the batsman is termed OUT. If none of the above conditions is met, the batsman is awarded some runs in the following way:

S1 = Sum of digits of the number on F

S2 = Sum of digits of the number on B

R(Runs awarded to the batsman) = Maximum(S1, S2)

After every turn, the card is put back into the deck, so that it can be picked again.

Each time the batsman picks a card, it is termed as a delivery(similar to cricket). Runs scored in each delivery keeps on adding to the total score of the batsman. So, the total score of a batsman is the sum of the runs scored by him/her in all the deliveries faced. The batsman keeps picking up cards till he/she is termed OUT. After the batsman is out, the second player follows the same till he/she is termed out. The player with a higher total score wins the game. A company sells four products A, B, C and D. The information about revenue, profit and total no of unit of the A, B,C and D have been shown using the pie charts (1), (2) and (3) respectively.

The profit is calculated using the following formula:

Profit = Revenue- Total Cost

Profit% = (Profit*100)/ Total Cost
questions.question_text: Which of the following has the maximum profit percentage among the following products?
questions.solution_text:
Assume the total revenue is 360R, the total profit is 360P and the total no of units is 360T.
Hence the profit for the product A is 96P, Revenue = 108R
Profit percentage for A = 96P*100/(108R-96P) = 100/(108R/96P-1) 
The profit for the product B is 84P, Revenue = 90R
Profit percentage for B = 84P*100/(90R-84P) = 100/(90R/84P-1)
The profit for the product C is 108P, Revenue = 72R
Profit percentage for C = 108P*100/(72R-108P) = 100/(72R/108P-1)
The profit for the product D is 72P, Revenue = 90R
Profit percentage for D = 72P*100/(90R-72P) = 100/(90R/72P-1)
Now, since 100/(72R/108P-1) denominator is lowest, the profit percentage should be the highest.
Hence C is the answer.

questions.question_text: If the total profit made on all the products is 33.33%, what is the ratio of the cost per unit of A to that of B?
questions.solution_text:
Assume the total revenue is 360R, the total profit is 360P and the total no of units is 360T.
Hence the profit for the product A is 96P, Revenue = 108R
Profit percentage for A = 96P*100/(108R-96P) = 100/(108R/96P-1) 
The profit for the product B is 84P, Revenue = 90R
Profit percentage for B = 84P*100/(90R-84P) = 100/(90R/84P-1)
The profit for the product C is 108P, Revenue = 72R
Profit percentage for C = 108P*100/(72R-108P) = 100/(72R/108P-1)
The profit for the product D is 72P, Revenue = 90R
Profit percentage for D = 72P*100/(90R-72P) = 100/(90R/72P-1)
 Now, the total profit made on all the products is 33.33%, Total Profit/ Total Cost = 360P/(360R-360P) = 33.33/100 
=> R=4P 
Cost per unit of A = Total cost for A/Total units of A  = (Total revenue - Total profit)/Total units of A = (108R-96P)/100T
Cost per unit of B = (Total revenue of B - Total profit of B)/(Total units of B) = (90R-84P)/80T
Ratio= ((108R-96P)/100T)/((90R-84P)/80T) =  $\frac{((108*4P-96P)*4)}{((90*4P-84P)*5)}$ = 112:115

The main tank releases 12,000 L of water daily, which gets distributed equally into the subsidiary tanks. The water that reaches the subsidiary tank, however, is less than the intended supply because of leakages. The amount of leakage is x% of the amount of water flowing through the pipe where x is the length of the pipe(in km). This leakage is also seen in the pipes joining the subsidiary tank and the mini tank and it varies in the same way as seen in the pipes joining the main tank and the subsidiary tank. In the case of the mini tanks, the water flowing from a subsidiary tank to each mini-tank connected to it is not equal. Had there has been no loss, the mini tank connected with the longest pipe gets 2 n + 1 \frac{2}{n+1} n + 1 2 ​ times the water released by the subsidiary tank (n is the number of mini-tanks connected to the subsidiary tank) and the other tanks get an equal amount of water. The diagram given below shows the length of the pipes in km. Some of the data is left blank intentionally.

X here is the main tank. P, Q and R are the subsidiary tanks and A, B, C, D, E, F and G are mini tanks. The numbers inside the oval boxes are the quantity of water received by the mini tanks. Burger + Pizza = 49
Burger can take value from (10,15,20), and the value of pizza has to be a prime number.
If Burger = 10, Pizza = 39 (Not prime)
If Burger = 15, Pizza = 34 (Not prime)
If Burger = 20, Pizza = 29 (prime and possible values)
Now, for Store 1.
Juice+Burger+Sandwich+Ice-Cream+Pizza = 110
Juice + Burger + 38+ Ice-Cream + 37 = 110
Juice + Burger + Ice-Cream = 35
Juice(4,8,16), Burger (10,15) and Ice-Cream (9,27)
Assuming Burger = 10
Juice + Ice- Cream = 25 (Possibility of Juice = 16 and Ice- Cream = 9)
If Burger = 15
Juice + Ice - Cream = 20 (No possible value of Juice and Ice-Cream possible)
Thus, for Store 1, Burger = 10, Juice = 16 and Ice- Cream = 9
Now, for Store 4, the number of burgers sold will be 15.
Juice+Burger+Sandwich+Ice-Cream+Pizza = 80
Juice + 15 +  14 + 36 + Pizza = 80
Juice + Pizza = 15
Now, we know the values of Pizza are  Prime numbers, so only Pizza = 11 is possible, then Juice = 4

Ram is a sales-man who has to travel to 7 cities for sales related work. The cities were named A, B, C, D, E, F and G. The map showing the position of the cities and the distances(in km) are as follows

Here the value above the line shows the direct distance between the 2 cities. For eg: the distance between city A and B is 12 km.
questions.question_text: What is the minimum distance Ram has to travel (in km) if he has to visit each city exactly once and return back to the starting city without using the same road twice?
questions.solution_text:
We observe that G has only 2 roads connected each to E or D.

If Ram starts from G, then he can either move towards E or D. Then he'll return to G via D or E respectively.

Thus we can say that D-G-E / E-G-D is a sure path. Since the question is about completing the round trip and not taking the same road or visiting a city twice let us assume Ram does D-G-E

From E ram can go to 3 different ways B, C or F

Case I: Ram goes to city B. Thus, the path will be D-G-E-B

Cities remaining to visit = A, C and F. But from B Ram can go towards either A or C.

If Ram goes A, then he has to go to C the+n F then D to complete the loop. The route becomes D-G-E-B-A-C-F-D.

If Ram goes towards C, then after that he can either go to A/F and then D. He'll miss 1 city in any case and hence not possible

Case II: Ram goes to city C. Thus, the path will be D-G-E-C

City remaining to visit = A, B and F

If Ram goes to A then the next city he has to go to is B. After which he can't go to F directly as there is no route. Thus this is not possible

If Ram goes to B then he can visit A next. After which again he can not reach F directly hence not possible

If Ram goes to F then he won't have a path to reach A/B without crossing an already visited city. Hence it is also not possible.

Case III: Ram goes to city F. Thus, the path becomes D-G-E-F

Remaining City = A, B and C.

From F, Ram has the only  option of going to C. Thus path becomes D-G-E-F-C

If from C Ram goes to A then the next city will be B. From which there is no other road directly to D. Thus, not possible

If from C Ram goes to B then the next city will be A. From which he'll go to D and complete the loop. D-G-E-F-C-B-A-D is possible

Overall 2 such loops are possible which are

i) D-G-E-B-A-C-F-D. Distance covered = 9+10+12+12+10+3+7 = 63 km

ii) D-G-E-F-C-B-A-D. Distance covered = 9+10+11+3+8+12+12 = 65 km

We are given that starting city is C and the last city is G. Let us make cases based on the number of intermediates cities( lets say N) Ram has to cross to reach G. Only way to reach G is via D or E

i) N =0. Since there are no direct road connecting C and G. Thus no case is possible.

ii) N = 1. There can be 1 intermediate city. Thus C-E-G and C-D-G are 2 possible cases

iii) N =2. There can be 2 intermediate city. Thus the possibilities are C-A-D-G, C-F-D-G, C-F-E-G and C-B-E-G

iv) N = 3. There can be 3 intermediate city. Possible cases are : C-B-A-D-G, C-E-F-D-G, C-D-F-E-G and C-A-B-E-G

v) N= 4. There are 4 intermediate cities(or exactly 1 city is not visited). Possible cases are : C-B-E-F-D-G, C-A-D-F-E-G, C-E-B-A-D-G and C-D-A-B-E-G

v) N=5, all 5 cities are visited. C-B-A-D-F-E-G, C-F-D-A-B-E-G, C-F-E-B-A-D-G, C-A-B-E-F-D-G are possible cases.

Total cases = 2+4+4+4+4 = 18

In row 1-1000 
In row 2-10 - 300 for window and 500 for aisle
In row 11 - 200 for window and 400 for aisle
In row 12,13 - 1000 
In row 14-20 - 200 for window and 400 for aisle
In row 21-30 - 0
Thus, As we can see 10, 11 and 12 are the only consecutive seats in which the amounts is different.
Thus, Jayanth, Ajit and Byomkesh sat in row 10, row 11 and row 12.
Manik sat beside Jayantha and thus Manik is also sitting in row 10.

It is obvious that 5 friends cannot pay 1000 Rs for their seat because the amount will exceed 4600

This is possible only when each of them pay 200 Rs.

Case 2 :- 3 friends pay 1000 Rs each. Thus, the remaining friends will pay 1600 Rs.
There are 2 cases where this is possible:-
1000*3, 500*2, 400, 200
1000*3, 400*4
Case 3:- 2 friends pay 1000 Rs each. Thus, the remaining 5 friends will pay 2600 Rs.
This is not possible as each friend can pay a maximum of 500 Rs.

1000*4 , 200*3
1000*3, 500*2, 400, 200
1000*3, 400*4
As there is no case in which a friend has to pay 300 Rs thus, Jayantha must be sitting in row 10 aisle seat.

1000*3, 500*2, 400, 200
Thus, Manik must have also paid 500 sitting in row 10 aisle seat
Ajit must be sitting in row 11 aisle seat paying 400 Rs.
Byomyesh must be sitting row 12 aisle seat paying 1000 Rs.

Among Pradosh and Tapesh a maximum of 1 person could have paid 1000 Rs.
Thus, the only possible case here is :- 
Gargi and Kikira paid 1000 each.
Pradosh is sitting ahead of Tapesh and one of them paid 200 Rs.

A shopkeeper sells three types of products A, B, and C over three days. The cost price of all three types products are constant over three days, while the selling price varies but selling prices are always greater than C.P. All the selling prices are multiples of 10.

1) The selling price for each particular product is in AP over three days, with one of those products having a decreasing AP.

2) On day 1, the profit percent on product A and product C is same.

3) On day 2,  the profit percent on product A and product B is same.

4) The profit obtained upon selling one B-product on day 2 is Rs. 50 more than the profit obatained upon selling one C-product on day 1.

5) The profit percentage on day-1 for product B is 30%.
questions.question_text: What is the average of C's selling price over three days?
questions.solution_text:
Let the cost prices (CP) of products A, B, and C be a, b, and c, respectively.
We are told that the selling prices of all three products are in AP over three days.
So, the selling price of the product on day 3 will be 140+20 = Rs. 160.
Statement 2: On day 1, the profit percent on product A and product C is the same.
If the profit percent is p, S.P of A will be $\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)\cdot a$ and S.P of C will be $\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)\cdot c$.
The ratio of these two will be a:c = 120:180 = 2:3
Similarly, considering statement 3:
If the profit percent is p, S.P of A will be $\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)\cdot a$ and S.P of B will be $\left(1+\frac{p}{100}\right)\cdot b$.
The ratio of these two will be a:b. And this is equal to 140:280 = 1:2
So, the C.Ps of A, B, and C are in the ratio 2:4:3. Let the C.Ps be 2k, 4k, and 3k, respectively.
We are told that the profit obtained upon selling one B-product on day 2 is Rs. 50 more than the profit obtained upon selling one C-product on day 1.
The profit obtained from selling 1 B-product on day 2 is 280 - 4k. And the profit obtained from selling one C-product on day 1 is 180 - 3k.
So, 280 - 4k = 50 + 180 - 3k
k = 50
So, the C.P of A, B and C will be 100, 200, and 150, respectively.
Considering statement 5, the S.P. for product B on day 1 will be 260.
So, product B is also having increasing S.P. We are told that one product is in decreasing AP. So, it has to be C.
It is mentioned in the question that selling prices are always greater than C.P. All the selling prices are multiples of 10. The only possible S.P. for product C will be Rs. 180, Rs. 170, and Rs. 160 for day 1, day 2, and day 3, respectively.
The average of selling prices of product C over 3 days is ₹170.

In numerology, the name and its associated numerical value hold significant importance as they are believed to shape a person's entire life. Specific numbers, including the Destiny number, Life path number and angel number, are calculated using the following methods:

Every Alphabet is assigned a number as follows - A = 1, B = 2,.......Y = 25 and Z = 26

We'll use the name "Jasmine" as an example, with numerical values assigned to each letter: 

J - 10, A - 1, S - 19, M - 13, I - 9, N - 14, E - 5.

Destiny number = 10 + 1 + 19 + 13 + 9 + 14 + 5 = 71 =  7 + 1 = 8   (Add until a single digit is obtained)

Life Path number = 10 * 1 * 19 * 13 * 9 * 14 * 5 = $2^2\times\ 3^2\times\ 5\times\ 7\times\ 13\times\ 19$ 

(Life Path number is the highest power of any prime number within this prime factorisation, which, in this case, is 2.)

Angel number is the highest prime number within the prime factorization, which in this example is 19.

Eight individuals, namely Robert, Patrick, Amanda, Joseph, Charles, Michael, Jessica, and Monica, consulted a numerologist with the intention of having them categorised as friends and partners and predicting their future.

1. If the destiny number of both individuals is a prime number, they will be friends.

2. If the destiny number of both individuals is equal to 1, they will be partners.

3. If the life path number is 3 or 5, the person will become a politician, and if it is an even number, the person will become an actor.

4. If the number of factors obtained by the multiplication of digits corresponding to the alphabets are the same, then they are called a super pair.

Six prominent e-commerce companies, namely Amazon, Flipkart, Alibaba, Snapdeal, Paytm Mall, and eBay, have collaborated to provide comprehensive data on the number of orders placed per day (in thousands) across a five-day period: Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. The data is visually represented in graphs, enabling a thorough analysis of consumer buying trends across different platforms.
To delve deeper into the analysis, a second graph displays the revenue generated (in millions of Rs.) by these orders for each specific day and platform. This visual representation allows for a comparative assessment of revenue performance among the e-commerce giants.
One crucial aspect being examined is the average order value, calculated by dividing the total revenue generated by the total number of orders placed. This metric serves as an indicator of the typical amount customers spend per order and aids in evaluating the overall profitability of the e-commerce platforms.
questions.question_text: Company "X" has the highest average order value amongst all the e-commerce companies on any day, What is the total revenue generated by Company X on Saturday and Sunday (in millions of Rs.)?
questions.solution_text:
Tabulating the data represented from the given two graphs-
Table-1 represents the number of orders(in thousands) across different e-commerce platforms on different days
Table-2 represents the revenue generated from the orders on different e-commerce platforms on different days
It is given that company "X" has the highest average order value amongst all the e-commerce companies on any day,
Average order value = Revenue / Number of orders
Therefore, the company with the least number of orders and maximum amount of revenue compared to others will have the highest average order value.
From the table, it can be inferred that Paytm Mall had the least number of orders (10 thousand) and revenue is (Rs. 50 million) on Thursday.
Therefore, the average order value = 50 million / 10 thousand = Rs.5000 per order
All other orders are 20 thousand or more. For the average order amount to be more than Rs.5000, the revenue should be more than 100 million; otherwise, it will be less than Rs. 5000. And, no company has a revenue of more than 100 million.
Thus, Paytm Mall is company "X"
So, the total revenue generated by Company X on Saturday and Sunday (in millions of Rs.) = 30+50 = 80

questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of ice creams that Varun can sell in a day?
questions.solution_text:
We know that the cost of a Vanilla ice cream is Rs. 3. Therefore, when a kid gives a 10 rupee note to Varun, he has to return 7 rupees as change. A chocolate ice cream costs 6 rupees and Varun has to return 4 rupees as change. A Pista ice cream costs Rs. 7. Varun has to return 3 rupees as change.   

We have to find the maximum number of ice creams that Varun can sell in a day.
To sell the maximum number of ice creams, Varun has to return the least number of coins possible to each kid. 

Also, we have to ensure that all the coins are used as evenly as possible. 

Each ice cream requires at least 2 coins to be delivered as change. The best way to deliver Rs.7 to kids who buy Vanilla ice cream is to give them a five rupee and two rupee coin. The best way to deliver Rs. 4 to kids who buy Chocolate ice cream is to give them 2 two rupee coins. The best way to deliver Rs. 3 to kids who buy Pista ice cream is to give them 1 one rupee and 1 two rupee coin. 

We have to select the ice creams such that we use all types of coins available with us. 

Varun could have sold 100 Vanilla ice creams by giving a five rupee coin and a two rupee coin to kids who bought the ice cream. If we provide 2 one rupee coins instead of 1 two rupee coins, then the number of Vanilla ice creams that can be sold will become 50 and the entire 5 rupee bundle cannot be used. Therefore, Varun has to return Rs. 7 as 1 five rupee coin and 1 two rupee coins. After selling 100 ice creams, Varun would have exhausted five rupee and two rupee coins. He will have 100 one rupee coins with him. If Varun sells Chocolate ice creams, he has to hand over 4 coins to every kid. If Varun sells Pista ice creams, he has to hand over 3 coins to every kid. Therefore, Varun can sell [100/3] = 33 Pista ice creams in addition to the 100 Vanilla ice creams. 

Therefore, the maximum number of ice creams that Varun could have sold is 100+33 = 133.

MakeMyTrip is surveying 160 premium members to track their interest in visiting Paris, New York, and Tokyo. They come to the realisation that the following conditions hold: 
1. More people were interested in visiting Paris than New York, and more people were interested in visiting New York than Tokyo
2. The number of people interested in visiting at most two destinations is three times that of those interested in visiting exactly three.
3. Exactly 50 people were interested in visiting exactly one destination. 
4. The number of people interested in visiting exactly two destinations is at least 20.

Using the given information, answer the following questions.
questions.question_text: What is the maximum number of people interested in visiting none of the destinations?
questions.solution_text:
Let us define the following variables, 
$A$=Number of people interested in visiting exactly one destination
$B$=Number of people interested in visiting exactly two destinations
$C$=Number of people interested in visiting exactly three destinations
$D$=Number of people interested in visiting exactly zero destinations
We are given that the number of people interested in visiting at most two destinations is thrice the number of people interested in visiting all three destinations.
Equating that, we get, 
$D+A+B=3C$
We also know that $D+A+B+C=160$
Substituting the value of $D+A+B$ we have $4C=160$ or $C=40$
Now we know that, $C=40$ and $A=50$
Substituting these values in the equation, $D+A+B=3C$, we have, 
$D+50+B=120$
$D+B=70$
$D=70-B$
The question asks us to maximise $D$, that means we will have to minimise $B$
The minimum value $B$ can take will be 20 since we are told that at least 20 people were interested in visiting exactly two destinations. 
Hence, $D=70-20$, $D=50$
The maximum possible number of people interested in visiting none of the three destinations is 50.
We can see from the subsequent questions that this is a possible scenario satisfying all the conditions given in the problemset.
